newsitem.title: USA: No new flood risk seen for lower Mississippi.
newsitem.headline: No new flood risk seen for lower Mississippi.

text.p: The heavy flooding that has battered the Northern Plains this week poses little threat to maritime operations on the lower Mississippi River, officials said on Tuesday.
"We're not expecting problems releated to the flooding in the Northwest," a U.S. Army Corps of Engineers spokesman in New Orleans said.
"We are expecting the river to rise a bit, but nothing like the high waters that we just got through with," he added.
Massive flooding along the Red River in North Dakota has wreaked havoc there in recent days, inundating 90 percent of the city of Grand Forks.

Maritime officials had initially feared melting snow in the Upper Midwest might also cause waters to swell on the lower Mississippi, which has yet to recover from a surge in floodwaters last month. But officials said today the longer-term threat to the Mississippi appeared negligible.

On Monday, the Coast Guard suspended nearly all of the navigation curbs it had imposed last month on the lower Mississippi, citing calmer waters. Maritime transit had been disrupted for weeks, as dangerously swift currents forced the Coast Guard to limit the size and speed of vessel traffic.
Despite the restrictions, surging floodwaters caused numerous accidents involving both barges and larger vessels.
The Coast Guard said that while it was unlikely any of the extensive curbs on shipping would be reinstated, a few moderate restrictions were possible.

Meanwhile, water levels on the lower Mississippi continued to decline, falling by more than half a foot overnight at Baton Rouge, Louisiana, to 35.2 feet. While down sharply from the river's 43 foot crest late last month, levels were still some six to seven feet above normal readings for this time of year, officials said.
The river also dropped farther south at New Orleans, falling to 14.3 feet this morning from 14.5 feet on Monday.
((-- Wendy Pollack, New York Commodities Desk +1 212 859 1640))
